state.task: We're rolling out a new multi-region e-commerce platform and I need help writing the Kubernetes manifests for our checkout service at `~/repos/shopstream-platform/k8s/`. The service is a Go application packaged as `shopstream/checkout-svc:1.4.2`. Here's what we need: a Deployment with 3 replicas using a rolling update strategy (maxSurge 1, maxUnavailable 0), resource requests of 256Mi memory / 250m CPU and limits of 512Mi / 500m, readiness and liveness probes hitting `/healthz` on port 8080, a HorizontalPodAutoscaler targeting 70% CPU utilization scaling between 3 and 12 replicas, a PodDisruptionBudget ensuring at least 2 pods are always available, and a Service of type ClusterIP. The pods need to pull config from a ConfigMap called `checkout-config` and secrets from a Secret called `checkout-secrets` mounted as environment variables. We also need pod anti-affinity rules so replicas spread across availability zones (labeled `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`), and the Deployment should have a `topologySpreadConstraints` block to enforce even distribution. Finally, add resource quotas for the `checkout` namespace limiting total CPU to 8 cores and memory to 16Gi. Please generate all the YAML files with comments explaining the production rationale behind each configuration choice.

state.task: Our team maintains an internal developer portal at `~/repos/dev-portal-docs` (MkDocs with Material theme, Python 3.11, mike for versioning) that builds API reference docs from OpenAPI specs and architecture decision records written in Markdown. The whole docs pipeline runs inside WSL2 Ubuntu 22.04 — we have a GitHub Actions self-hosted runner there that triggers `mkdocs build`, runs link checkers, and publishes to our internal static site host. Right now the setup is a mess: the MkDocs plugins (`mkdocs-awesome-pages`, `mkdocs-macros`, `mkdocs-redirects`) were installed ad-hoc with pip instead of through our `pyproject.toml`, the `mike` versioning aliases are broken so `/latest` 404s, and the GitHub Actions runner service isn't set up as a proper systemd unit so it dies after reboot. Also, our team uses a shared profile convention where each developer's WSL environment reads machine-specific config from `/mnt/c/Users/user/.admin/profiles/{hostname}.json` — that profile includes things like the docs deploy target URL, the GitHub token variable name, and preferred Python version. I need you to: (1) read my machine's profile JSON and use its settings throughout, (2) set up a proper `pyproject.toml` with uv for all MkDocs dependencies and pin versions, (3) fix the `mike` versioning so that `latest` and `stable` aliases work correctly in our `mkdocs.yml`, (4) create a systemd user service for the GitHub Actions runner so it auto-starts on WSL boot, (5) write a `docs-ci.sh` script that the runner calls which does a clean build, runs `htmltest` for broken links, validates the OpenAPI specs with `vacuum`, and deploys the versioned site, and (6) add a pre-commit hook that catches broken cross-references before they hit CI. Can you walk me through all of this and generate the config files?

state.task: Can you help me define the data models for our veterinary clinic's appointment scheduling API? We need a `Pet` model with species, breed, name, date_of_birth (optional), and weight in kg (must be positive), a `VetDoctor` model with license_number validated against a regex pattern like `VET-\d{6}`, list of specializations, and availability windows, and an `Appointment` model that references both with start/end datetimes where end must be after start, an enum status field (scheduled/completed/cancelled/no_show), and an optional notes field max 500 chars. Each model should have proper examples in the JSON schema, and I'd like a `ClinicConfig` model using `model_config` for environment-based settings like db connection string, max daily appointments per vet (default 20), and cancellation window hours. Also add a custom validator on Appointment that raises an error if someone tries to book outside the vet's availability windows.

The stack will be a Python/FastAPI backend with a React/TypeScript frontend using TanStack Query. I need three things done: First, set up the Python project from scratch using `uv` for dependency management, with a proper `pyproject.toml`, a shared `utils/` package for database helpers and date/season calculations, and a `scripts/` directory following our team's convention of prefixing scripts with `run_` and including a `if __name__ == "__main__"` guard. Second, write a detailed requirements specification for the "Field Entry Submission" feature — this is where farmers submit daily yield data for their assigned fields. I need proper user stories with acceptance criteria, edge cases (offline submissions, duplicate entries, conflicting data from shared fields), and clearly defined system behaviors for validation, conflict resolution, and notification triggers. Make the requirements testable and unambiguous so QA can derive test cases directly. Third, on the React side, when a farmer submits a new yield entry via the form, I want the entry to appear immediately in the daily yields table and update the running season total in the sidebar — don't wait for the server round-trip. If the mutation fails (network error, validation rejection, conflict detected), roll back the table row and season total to their previous state, show a toast explaining what went wrong, and if it was a conflict, pre-fill the form again with the farmer's original input so they don't lose their data. I want the optimistic state managed through TanStack Query's mutation lifecycle hooks rather than manual state juggling.

state.task: We're starting a new internal tool called "HarvestBoard" — a crop yield tracking dashboard for our agricultural cooperative. The stack will be a Python/FastAPI backend with a React/TypeScript frontend using TanStack Query. I need three things done: First, set up the Python project from scratch using `uv` for dependency management, with a proper `pyproject.toml`, a shared `utils/` package for database helpers and date/season calculations, and a `scripts/` directory following our team's convention of prefixing scripts with `run_` and including a `if __name__ == "__main__"` guard. Second, write a detailed requirements specification for the "Field Entry Submission" feature — this is where farmers submit daily yield data for their assigned fields. I need proper user stories with acceptance criteria, edge cases (offline submissions, duplicate entries, conflicting data from shared fields), and clearly defined system behaviors for validation, conflict resolution, and notification triggers. Make the requirements testable and unambiguous so QA can derive test cases directly. Third, on the React side, when a farmer submits a new yield entry via the form, I want the entry to appear immediately in the daily yields table and update the running season total in the sidebar — don't wait for the server round-trip. If the mutation fails (network error, validation rejection, conflict detected), roll back the table row and season total to their previous state, show a toast explaining what went wrong, and if it was a conflict, pre-fill the form again with the farmer's original input so they don't lose their data. I want the optimistic state managed through TanStack Query's mutation lifecycle hooks rather than manual state juggling.

state.task: We're starting a new internal tool called "HarvestBoard" — a crop yield tracking dashboard for our agricultural cooperative. The stack will be a Python/FastAPI backend with a React/TypeScript frontend using TanStack Query. I need three things done: First, set up the Python project from scratch using `uv` for dependency management, with a proper `pyproject.toml`, a shared `utils/` package for database helpers and date/season calculations, and a `scripts/` directory following our team's convention of prefixing scripts with `run_` and including a `if __name__ == "__main__"` guard. Second, write a detailed requirements specification for the "Field Entry Submission" feature — this is where farmers submit daily yield data for their assigned fields. I need proper user stories with acceptance criteria, edge cases (offline submissions, duplicate entries, conflicting data from shared fields), and clearly defined system behaviors for validation, conflict resolution, and notification triggers. Make the requirements testable and unambiguous so QA can derive test cases directly. Third, on the React side, when a farmer submits a new yield entry via the form, I want the entry to appear immediately in the daily yields table and update the running season total in the sidebar — don't wait for the server round-trip. If the mutation fails (network error, validation rejection, conflict detected), roll back the table row and season total to their previous state, show a toast explaining what went wrong, and if it was a conflict, pre-fill the form again with the farmer's original input so they don't lose their data. I want the optimistic state managed through TanStack Query's mutation lifecycle hooks rather than manual state juggling.

state.task: Our "AquaVault" water treatment monitoring backend (FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Celery workers) just had a rough deploy — the `alembic upgrade head` migration is failing with a locked advisory lock error, the Celery beat scheduler can't find the `redis` package even though it's in our Poetry lockfile, and our `/api/v2/sensors/readings` endpoint is throwing 500s because of a missing `pydantic` validator import. I need you to get the service back to a healthy state by running the deploy steps in a loop that detects and auto-fixes these kinds of issues (retry migrations on lock conflicts, install missing deps if they're not resolving, fix broken imports), escalating anything truly unexpected. Once you've stabilized things, write up full documentation for the new `v2/sensors` module following our repo's `DOCUMENTATION_GUIDELINES.md` — it should include the architecture overview, all endpoint contracts with request/response payloads, a Mermaid sequence diagram showing the flow from sensor ingestion through Celery task processing to database persistence, and the seeding instructions for populating test sensor data. Log everything significant you do during recovery and documentation into our `JOURNAL.md` so the on-call team has a record of what happened and what was fixed.

state.task: Our research group built a static analysis tool in C that we need compiled with CompCert (the formally verified C compiler) to satisfy our certification requirements, and we're hitting dependency hell trying to get it built from source on Ubuntu 22.04 — Coq version mismatches, OCaml/opam issues, and the build keeps getting killed (probably OOM on our 8GB CI runners). Can you walk us through the full build process with the right pinned dependency versions and memory workarounds? Also, once the tool is compiled, we need to ship it with a lightweight web-based report viewer that researchers can open in a browser to inspect the analysis results — think a single-page dashboard with a sidebar listing source files, a main panel showing annotated C code with highlighted warnings, and a collapsible detail drawer for each finding. We want the UI to feel clean and professional but also scannable for someone reviewing hundreds of findings. Can you help us nail down both the CompCert build pipeline and the design direction for the report viewer (layout structure, color strategy for severity levels, typography choices for code vs. prose, etc.)?

Covers OCaml/opam setup, Coq version compatibility, memory management, and common build pitfalls.

state.task: We're designing a multi-agent customer support system for our insurance platform using Microsoft's Agent Framework (with `autogen-agentchat` and `autogen-ext`). The plan is to have four specialized agents — PolicyLookup, ClaimsProcessor, BillingAssistant, and EscalationCoordinator — orchestrated by a central GroupChat manager. PolicyLookup should call our internal REST API to fetch policy details, ClaimsProcessor needs to invoke an Azure Function for damage assessment, and EscalationCoordinator should route unresolved conversations to a human agent via our ServiceNow integration. Can you scaffold the full project structure with concrete agent definitions, tool registrations for each external service, the GroupChat orchestration config with a custom speaker-selection strategy (claims questions go to ClaimsProcessor first, billing to BillingAssistant, and anything mentioning "cancel" or "complaint" immediately to EscalationCoordinator), and a FastAPI wrapper that accepts incoming chat messages and streams agent responses back via SSE? Also include proper termination conditions so the conversation ends when the customer confirms resolution or after three consecutive EscalationCoordinator turns without human pickup.

Since last Thursday, the dashboard's "Tüketim Tahmin" (consumption forecast) panel is rendering but showing completely empty cards — no numbers, no charts, just the skeleton UI with a small gray text that says "Şu anda spesifik bilgi mevcut değil" ("no specific information available at this time"). The weird part is: (1) our backend logs show 200 responses from the EPİAŞ endpoint, (2) if I hit our `/api/v1/consumption/realtime` endpoint directly with curl I get what looks like valid JSON with actual MWh figures, and (3) the other panels (generation, price) work fine. I traced it into the frontend and the React component `ConsumptionForecastCard.tsx` is receiving props, but somewhere between the data fetch hook (`useConsumptionData.ts`) and the rendering, it falls through to a fallback/stub message. This started right after we merged PR #847 which refactored how we normalize the UEÇM response schema — the new `normalizeUECM()` function in `utils/consumption.ts` was supposed to handle both the old and new EPİAŞ payload formats. Can you help me build a minimal deterministic reproduction (maybe a Vitest test) that isolates exactly where the fallback gets triggered, figure out why `normalizeUECM()` silently returns an empty result instead of throwing, and fix it so the real-time consumption and demand forecast data renders correctly again? I also want to make sure the load plan (yük planı) tab that we're building next sprint won't hit the same silent-fallback issue.

state.task: We're spinning up a new "RetainIQ" project for our customer success team — it's a Python service that monitors product usage signals (like declining logins, feature drop-off, license underutilization, contract renewal dates) and automatically triggers the right retention or expansion playbook from a catalog we maintain. I need two things: first, set up the dev environment from scratch — Python 3.12 with Poetry, pre-commit hooks, a Dockerfile for local development, VS Code workspace settings with recommended extensions (Ruff, mypy, Python Test Explorer), and a Makefile with common commands so new CS engineers can onboard quickly. Second, design the data model and storage layer for our playbook catalog — each play should be tagged with the signal that triggers it (e.g., "usage_drop_30d", "nps_detractor", "seat_utilization_below_40pct"), the target cohort (enterprise vs. SMB, tenure bucket, ARR tier), whether it's a churn-prevention or expansion play, the sequence of actions (email template, CSM task, in-app message), and success metrics we track against it. I want to be able to query things like "show me all expansion plays for enterprise accounts with seat utilization above 80% that were triggered in Q3" or "which churn plays have the best save rate for SMB accounts in their first 90 days." Scaffold the project structure, write the SQLAlchemy models, and include a seed script with at least 10 realistic example plays covering a mix of churn and expansion scenarios across different cohorts and signals.
